queue.title: A Supplier Who Does Not Share Data Is Not a Partner
queue.content:
A partnership without transparent data exchange remains just a formal contract, not real cooperation. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A partnership without transparent exchange of operational data remains just a formal contract, not real cooperation.

A partnership without transparent exchange of operational data remains just a formal contract, not real cooperation.

The label 'strategic partner' loses meaning when a supplier refuses to share the basic operational data needed for joint planning and risk management. The GNK DINAMO Ltd. Group distinguishes transactional suppliers from strategic partners precisely by the level of data transparency a relationship is willing to bear.

The level of transparency a supplier is willing to offer is usually a more reliable indicator of the future relationship than any clause in the contract itself.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

queue.title: Data Without an Owner Is Not an Asset
queue.content:
Data no one formally owns doesn't get maintained or verified, and becomes a risk over time. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Data no one formally owns doesn't get maintained, doesn't get verified, and over time becomes a risk instead of a value.

Data no one formally owns doesn't get maintained, doesn't get verified, and over time becomes a risk instead of a value.

Every dataset needs a named owner responsible for its accuracy, security, and purpose of use — without that, the data exists but no one actually maintains it. GNK ASG d.o.o. assigns clear responsibility for every publicly published data source before it's used in analytics or reporting.

In practice, this means every report, table, or dashboard should have a clearly named person accountable for its accuracy — not a department, but an individual who knows where the data comes from and how it's updated.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

queue.title: Cyber Insurance: Terms and Exclusions
queue.content:
A cyber insurance policy is only as good as how well its terms match real infrastructure, not a template. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A cyber insurance policy is only as good as how well its coverage terms actually match the company's real infrastructure, not a generic template.

A cyber insurance policy is only as good as how well its coverage terms actually match the company's real infrastructure, not a generic template.

Cyber policies often contain exclusions for 'known vulnerabilities' or 'lack of reasonable security practice' — wording the insurer interprets only after the damage occurs, when the company's negotiating position is weakest.

A requirement that systems be 'updated to industry standards' sounds reasonable, but without a concrete definition in the policy it opens room to deny a claim based on a subjective assessment.

Companies that conduct an internal compliance review against all stated terms before signing a policy avoid paying a premium for coverage that doesn't hold up in practice.

Regularly updating the policy as infrastructure changes is just as important as initially obtaining it; a policy based on an outdated system state carries a hidden risk of claim denial.
